--- title: "Data Transformation and Wrangling in R" date: "1/6/2025" date-modified: last-modified date-format: long --- # Data Transformation and Wrangling in R ## 1. Introduction ### Overview Data transformation and wrangling involve cleaning, reshaping, and modifying data to prepare it for analysis. This tutorial introduces: - **Base R Functions**: `subset()`, `transform()`, `merge()`. - **tidyverse Functions**: `dplyr::filter()`, `dplyr::mutate()`, `tidyr::pivot_longer()`, and others. ### Use Cases - Filtering rows based on conditions. - Adding or modifying columns. - Reshaping data between wide and long formats. - Combining or joining datasets. ### Benefits - **Base R**: Built into R, no additional installations required. - **tidyverse**: Consistent syntax and powerful chaining with the pipe operator `|>`. ## 2. Getting Started ### Loading the Package ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Base R requires no additional loading. # Load tidyverse package using pacman pacman::p_load(tidyverse) ``` ::: ## 3. Key Functions and Features ### Using Base R #### Filtering Rows **Description**: Extract rows based on a condition. **Syntax**: ```r subset(x, subset, select = NULL) ``` **Arguments**: - `x`: A data frame or similar object. - `subset`: Logical expression indicating rows to keep. - `select`: Columns to retain, or `NULL` to keep all. **Example**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data(iris) # Filter rows where Species is "setosa" subset(iris, Species == "setosa") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

::: ::: #### Modifying Columns **Description**: Add or modify columns in a data frame. **Syntax**: ```r transform(data, ...) ``` **Arguments**: - `data`: A data frame. - `…`: Expressions specifying transformations. **Example**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Add a new column for Sepal Area iris <- transform(iris, Sepal.Area = Sepal.Length * Sepal.Width) head(iris) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

::: ::: #### Joining Data **Description**: Combine datasets based on common columns (keys). **Syntax**: ```r merge(x, y, by, all) ``` **Arguments**: - `x`, `y`: Data frames to merge. - `by`: Column names to use as keys. Defaults to all common columns. - `all`: Logical. `TRUE` for full outer join; `FALSE` for inner join. **Example**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create example datasets df1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Value = c(10, 20, 30)) df2 <- data.frame(ID = 2:4, Score = c(15, 25, 35)) # Merge on ID merge(df1, df2, by = "ID") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| ID| Value| Score| |--:|-----:|-----:| | 2| 20| 15| | 3| 30| 25|

::: ::: ## 4. In-Depth Examples ### Example 1: Cleaning and Transforming Data **Objective**: Prepare `mtcars` for analysis by filtering rows, creating a new column, and summarizing data. **Steps**: 1. Filter cars with `mpg > 20`. 2. Add a column `Weight_kg` converting `wt` to kilograms. 3. Summarize average MPG by the number of cylinders. **Code**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Using Base R mtcars_filtered <- subset(mtcars, mpg > 20) mtcars_filtered <- transform(mtcars_filtered, Weight_kg = wt * 453.6) aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars_filtered, mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| cyl| mpg| |---:|--------:| | 4| 26.66364| | 6| 21.13333|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Using tidyverse mtcars |> dplyr::filter(mpg > 20) |> dplyr::mutate(Weight_kg = wt * 453.6) |> dplyr::group_by(cyl) |> dplyr::summarize(Average_MPG = mean(mpg)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| cyl| Average_MPG| |---:|-----------:| | 4| 26.66364| | 6| 21.13333|

Best Practices 1. Use **descriptive column names**. 2. Keep data in **tidy format** for easier analysis. 3. Prefer **tidyverse** for a consistent and readable workflow. ## 8.
